units.t: Space & Cosmos Shorts.
In this episode: First Nations astronomy.
Part one. First Nations astronomy.
Long before telescopes, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples read the night sky as a calendar, a map, a law book and a library of stories.
The oldest sky watchers.
Australia's First Peoples have lived on this continent for at least 50,000 years, and many researchers think longer.
For all that time they have looked up at the same southern sky, and their knowledge of it is woven through culture, law and daily life.
There is no single "Aboriginal astronomy".
Australia has hundreds of distinct nations and language groups, each with its own stories and ways of reading the sky, though some stories are shared across vast distances.
The stars were used to tell the seasons, find food, navigate, mark ceremonies and pass on rules for living.
Some of this knowledge is sacred and not for public sharing.
The Emu in the Sky.
Western constellations join up bright stars.
Many Aboriginal traditions also look at the spaces between them.
The best known example is the Emu in the Sky.
Its head is the Coalsack, a dark dust cloud beside the Southern Cross, and its neck, body and legs stretch along dark lanes in the Milky Way.
On autumn evenings, after dark, the emu appears to be running across the sky.
For a number of groups this coincides with the time emus are mating and laying eggs, a signal for when eggs could be collected.
Later in the year the emu's shape appears to change position, reflecting different stages of the breeding cycle.
The Seven Sisters.
The Pleiades, a small, tight cluster of stars, has inspired stories in cultures from ancient Greece to Japan.
In Australia it is the heart of the Seven Sisters, one of the most widespread and important Aboriginal stories.
In many desert versions, sisters are pursued across the country by a man, often linked to stars in the constellation Westerners call Orion.
As they flee, their journey creates and names features of the landscape, forming songlines: routes that link sites over thousands of kilometres and carry knowledge, law and ceremony.

In 2017 the National Museum of Australia staged Songlines: Tracking the Seven Sisters, developed with Anangu, Martu and Ngaanyatjarra communities and sharing parts of the story through paintings, song and dance.
Tagai and star calendars.
For Torres Strait Islanders, the most important sky figure is Tagai, a great fisherman standing in his canoe.
In common descriptions, his left hand holds a fishing spear, the Southern Cross, and his right hand holds a sorbi fruit, the stars of Corvus.
His canoe and crew are made of other stars.
Tagai teaches the importance of following rules and sharing, and his position guides when to plant, fish and hunt turtle and dugong.
Across Australia, stars appearing at dawn or dusk signal events on the ground.
In the 1850s William Stanbridge recorded Boorong knowledge in north-western Victoria, including stars used to mark the seasons for gathering food.
These calendars are tailored to local country, since seasons differ across Australia.
Tides, eclipses and respect.
Sky knowledge was not only stories; it recorded careful observations.
The Yolngu of north-east Arnhem Land link the tides to the Moon, describing the Moon filling with water as tides rise, which captures a real connection.
Several groups have stories explaining eclipses, often as the Sun woman and Moon man coming together.
Researchers have found traditions that appear to describe changing brightness in stars such as Betelgeuse and Antares, which astronomy recognises as variable.
Some scholars think stories about Wolfe Creek Crater may preserve memories of real events, though that is hard to prove.
To learn more, seek sources made by or with communities, such as Aboriginal-run tours and museum resources.
Stories differ between nations, and some knowledge is restricted.
The key idea: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have read the night sky for many thousands of years, with knowledge that differs between nations.

Answer. Hundreds of nations have their own sky stories.
